A reinforcement-learning policy adapts monitoring, access, deception, and segmentation under a safety-governance layer, reducing attack-path completion, detection, and containment versus static baselines.

items.title: An Incentive-Aligned Trust-Centric Coordination Layer for Heterogeneous Blockchain Interoperability
items.author: Saeed Moradi, Sara Rouhani
items.content: The interoperability between permissioned and public blockchains is hampered by asymmetric privacy, trust, and governance assumptions. We propose a coordination architecture that decouples cross-domain trust management and privacy enforcement from underlying blockchain protocols, requiring no protocol-level modifications. The framework integrates cryptographic unlinkability mechanisms with incentive-compatible relay selection, combining stake-weighted participation and temporally accumulated reputation to align economic commitment with sustained correctness. We formalize the adversarial model and derive security and privacy properties for cross-domain coordination, demonstrating robustness against Sybil infiltration, collusion, and strategic stake concentration. Simulation-based analysis characterizes key design trade-offs between quorum thresholds, reputation memory, and anonymity parameters, indicating that privacy-preserving coordination can be achieved without degrading responsiveness or incentive stability when parameters are properly tuned.

items.title: Closing the Applied Cybersecurity Gap in Critical Infrastructure: A Cyber-to-Physical Security Assessment Framework for Water Systems
items.author: Halil Dursunoglu, Kaan Sulkalar
items.content: The integration of information technology and operational technology in water infrastructure creates pathways through which cyber compromise may affect physical service delivery. This study revisits the Applied Cybersecurity Gap (ACG) framework by evaluating an experimental Applied Cybersecurity Gap Index (ACGI) alongside the Cyber-to-Physical Propagation Rate (CPPR), defined as the proportion of initially compromised trials that produce a specified physical-impact outcome. The expanded evaluation comprises 2,160 synthetic trials across three water-network benchmarks, including EPANET Example Network 3 (Net3), and couples declared cyber-attack progression rules with hydraulic simulations. A source-trained machine-learning model evaluated on 247 compromised Net3 trials achieved ROC-AUC 0.772, PR-AUC 0.775, and F1 0.733, compared with 0.661, 0.642, and 0.704 for a scenario-only baseline. The configuration-cluster bootstrap interval for the ROC-AUC difference was 0.038--0.183. A separate 720-run Net3 hydraulic operating-point sensitivity analysis achieved the study's exploratory baseline pressure criterion in all reruns, preserved 717 of 720 physical-impact labels, and produced ROC-AUC 0.791 with the frozen source-trained model. Additional analyses examine the sensitivity of CPPR to the physical-impact threshold and assumed control-blocking probabilities, and demonstrate that the ACGI--CPPR association is partly induced by the simulation design rather than independently validated. The findings establish a reproducible simulation-based assessment workflow, but do not constitute field calibration of cybersecurity-control effectiveness or prediction of real-world utility incidents.

items.title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
items.author: Runze Zhao, Dongruo Zhou, Sumit Kumar Jha, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Ankit Shah
items.content: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.

items.title: Evaluating Structural and SAT Attack Resilience in Cryptographic Dynamic Logic Locking via Keystream Capping
items.author: Nahush Tambe, Naseeruddin Lodge, Vineet Chadalavada, Fareena Saqib
items.content: Untrusted third-party entities throughout the semiconductor supply chain expose proprietary hardware intellectual property to reverse engineering, piracy, and overproduction. While logic locking counters this threat by embedding key-dependent logic, conventional static key-gates remain vulnerable to both oracle-guided SAT attacks and structural removal attacks due to their time-invariant netlist signatures. Dynamic schemes such as STREAMLOCK mitigate oracle attacks by continuously masking signals with cryptographic keystream, achieving near 50\% Hamming distance output corruption under incorrect keys with low hardware overhead. However, confining key-gates to primary outputs leaves internal combinational cones vulnerable to single-tap structural bypasses. This work extends dynamic logic locking by distributing key-gates within internal paths prioritized via fault-propagation analysis. The original and internally-hardened architectures are evaluated against structural removal attacks and a bounded, unrolling-based SAT-style attack across three ISCAS'85 benchmarks. Distributing masking internally raises the uninformed attacker's brute-force search space from 6 candidate node subsets to over $10^{45}$ for the largest benchmark. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals that topological relocation alone does not prevent algebraic key extraction when wide circuits expose numerous keystream bits per clock cycle. To eliminate this leak, a keystream-bit reuse cap is introduced to restrict per-cycle exposure independent of circuit width. Under this constraint, SAT-solver tractability encounters an immediate computational cliff, transitioning sharply from rapid under-constrained solving to timeout thresholds without disclosing the secret key. Integrating fault-aware internal placement with keystream reuse capping delivers joint resilience against structural bypasses and bounded SAT attacks.

items.title: AIFaultBench: A Reproducible Benchmark of Real-World Faults in AI Software Systems
items.author: Mehil B Shah, Mohammad Masudur Rahman, Foutse Khomh
items.content: AI-based software systems remain difficult to debug because their failures can involve interactions among code, models, data, dependencies, hardware, and execution environments. Existing benchmarks cover specific classes of AI systems, while concerns about fault realism and reproducibility highlight the need for documented execution conditions and evidence. We present AIFaultBench, a benchmark of 770 real-world bugs from 105 AI-based software repositories across 76 organizations. It covers six classes of AI systems: machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, systems based on large language models, agentic AI, and AI tooling and infrastructure. Each bug record connects the original report and affected codebase to structured metadata, environment setup scripts, a reproduction trigger, and investigation evidence. We reproduced 652 bugs (84.7%) under the recorded execution conditions and documented the outcomes of the remaining 118 attempts. Through its broad coverage, documented reproduction evidence, and common structure, AIFaultBench supports empirical studies of AI faults, debugging tool evaluation, practical failure investigation, and teaching with real-world examples.

items.title: RepGen: Reproducing Deep Learning Bugs through Context-Aware Code Generation and Verification
items.author: Mehil B Shah, Mohammad Masudur Rahman, Foutse Khomh
items.content: Reproducing deep learning (DL) bugs is challenging because failures can involve source code, models, data, dependencies, and execution environments. Incomplete bug reports further complicate reproduction by omitting essential details. We present RepGen, an open-source tool for reproducing DL bugs through context-aware code generation and iterative verification. Given a bug report and repository, RepGen explores the codebase to build a learning-enhanced context, develop a reproduction plan, and generate candidate scripts. It refines candidates using static checks and LLM feedback to improve their correctness and relevance. When enabled, the tool prepares the execution environment, runs the script, and assesses its output against the reported failure. RepGen provides an interactive command-line interface supporting local and hosted LLMs, configurable execution budgets, and inspectable artifacts, along with a GitHub Action for automated issue processing. The underlying approach reproduced 85 of 106 real-world DL bugs (80.19%). A controlled study with 27 developers showed a 23.35% improvement in reproduction success and a 56.8% reduction in reproduction time.

items.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
items.author: Junyu Huo, Zihao Wan, Ziqi Mao, Gouri Ginde
items.content: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.

items.title: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum
items.author: Ziwei Li, Tianwei Chen, Jiajing Wu, Zigui Jiang, Yuhong Nan, Yaobo Huang, Bowen Song, Zibin Zheng
items.content: EIP-7702 introduces a new transaction type that allows Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) on major EVM-compatible chains to delegate execution to arbitrary contract codes temporarily. While enhancing functionality, this mechanism facilitates a novel threat: the \underline{E}IP-7702-Based \underline{E}ther \underline{R}edirection \underline{A}ttack (EERA). In such an attack, a victim is delegated to a malicious sweeper contract, which automatically redirects incoming ETH transfers to an address controlled by the attacker. As a nascent attack paradigm arising from protocol evolution, the underlying mechanisms and security implications of EERA remain systematically unexplored. To bridge this gap, we provide the first formal analysis of the EERA attack model and propose SweeperHunter, a framework that detects these attacks through transaction analysis. By evaluating transactions from the first ten months following the introduction of EIP-7702 on Ethereum mainnet, we have identified 4,668,209 malicious delegations, 20,443 attack transactions and 508 ETH sweeper contracts, forming the first EERA dataset. Finally, we analyze this attack from both attacker and victim perspectives, derive key insights, and propose corresponding mitigation strategies. We reveal the prevalence of EERA, as approximately 70\% of the observed delegations point toward ETH sweeper contracts. Furthermore, we observe a notable lack of effective responses from victims; specifically, over 600,000 accounts failed to revoke or update their malicious delegations promptly, thereby remaining in a state of vulnerability. Our research is expected to facilitate understanding and mitigation of this emerging threat posed by EIP-7702.

items.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
items.author: Shanglin Yang, Zhan Shi
items.content: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.

items.title: ROSTrans: Empirically Benchmarking LLMs for ROS1-to-ROS2 Migration
items.author: Yichen Zhao, Minghao Shao, Zhuoyan Yu, Yijun Shen, Boyuan Chen, Yik-Cheung Tam, Muhammad Shafique
items.content: Although large language models have shown strong capabilities in domain-specific code generation, their performance in robotics software development, especially for the Robot Operating System (ROS), remains largely unexplored. ROS code generation presents distinctive challenges, including complex inter-node coordination, middleware configuration, and lifecycle semantics that go far beyond standard coding benchmarks, and many important correctness properties become observable only once migrated nodes are launched and communicate. We present ROSTrans, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 code migration, a representative and practically important setting for ROS code generation. ROSTrans comprises 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from a diverse set of 70+ open-source ROS1 repositories and organized into a hierarchical taxonomy assessing interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness. For every task we establish an executable reference: a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises their topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container ensuring reproducibility. Candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into an otherwise fixed copy of the reference package, so a candidate can neither supply nor weaken the tests it is judged by. Evaluating six frontier LLMs over five stochastic generations per task, we find pass@1 below 10.9%, and that 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime,and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, a class of error no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair further improves task success, reaching 49.1% and 47.2% for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds, respectively.

items.title: More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year
items.author: Marlize van Romburgh
items.content: Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3. Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups. Large rounds dominate funding One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more. As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023. The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds. Deals keep falling even as dollars rise In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared. In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year. The early-stage slump Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low. It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips. Looking ahead Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom. A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure. But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars. items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.content: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434. The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. items.title: How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
items.author: Alex Fattouche
items.content: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver. In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge. We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver. How DNS changes reach the edge A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network. A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting. The change is stored in a database. The database change or another system produces a Kafka event. The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder. The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers. The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver, our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network. This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly. Why full builds stopped scaling The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state. Read the current zone and its settings. Read every DNS record in the zone. Convert those records into Quicksilver keys. Compare the new keys with those already stored. Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata. The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below. Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com. CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain. A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions: Which DNS names can change? Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change? What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver? Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order: Events had to say what changed. Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct. Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name. The database could change between the event and the build. Combining work could not lose a Kafka message. Making events say what changed We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect. Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again. Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work. Choosing the smallest safe build Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both. With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types: Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path. Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path. Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path. Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published. Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe. The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build. Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write. Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time. There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone. When one name means more than one zone Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query. Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish. Consider four internal zones for example.com: Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name. A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key. At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them. Planning from the event, verifying before writing An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network. Fresh state can change the result in four ways: A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work. A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network. A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key. A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set. The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind. Combining changes in one scheduler Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run. When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work: An A record changes at www.example.com, requiring that name. A wildcard changes at *.example.com, requiring that name and shared metadata. The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build. Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published. The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written. Keeping Kafka moving One slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart. We use soft committing, which I previously described in my Secondary DNS deep dive. A build can finish out of order and be marked complete in memory, but Kafka's committed position advances only after every earlier message has also finished. In the diagram, message 2 is still running, so messages 3 through n cannot be committed. If the Zone Builder restarts, those in-memory completions disappear and Kafka replays messages 2 through n. We deliberately choose repeated work over losing a change. Targeted plans reduce how long the oldest message stays unfinished. The scheduler also prevents one busy zone from taking every worker. After a zone builds, its next build waits for a per-zone rebuild interval, which differs by Cloudflare plan. Changes that arrive in the meantime are merged into that next build. The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop. Releasing safely A smaller build is useful only if it produces the same DNS data. We added equivalence tests for nameserver, wildcard, and apex paths. Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation. During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence. Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic. A comparer checks a 20% sample of zones for missing keys, extra keys, and different values. The two environments do not always build a zone at the same instant, so a temporary mismatch is not automatically a regression. We look for new types of differences that remain after both pipelines catch up. That gives us confidence that targeted builds produce the same output as production. We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. Naturally, it runs on the Cloudflare Developer Platform: a Worker receives results, Durable Objects maintain state, and Cloudflare Access protects it. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears. After the mirror results remained healthy, we rolled the scheduler out by a hash of the zone name. Hashing the name rather than the zone ID kept every zone sharing a name on the same scheduler, so two schedulers never wrote the same metadata key. We increased the percentage for free zones, then repeated the process for paid zones. Results Over 24 hours, we measured 86.81% of builds as resources only, 2.54% as resources and metadata, 2.30% as apex and metadata, and 1.30% as purges. Together, 92.95% of builds avoided rebuilding the complete zone. Full builds were the remaining 7.04%. The two metadata build types were full builds before, even for large zones. Together, they account for 4.84% of builds. Combined with the 7.04% that are still full builds, that is 11.88%, so full builds fell by about 40%. Their share of the count also understates the work avoided, because they include the largest zones. The full builds that remain average 0.35 seconds, because the events that still trigger them, such as a zone being published for the first time, mostly affect new zones with few records. In 2022, we also planned a batching system. The unified scheduler makes it unnecessary: it does not wait to form batches, and it merges events only when work is already queued for the same zone. Before, long full builds held back the committed offset for their partition. With fewer of them, we now consume Kafka at the rate events arrive, instead of falling behind and catching up in bursts of up to 1,550 messages per second. We also measured build completion delay: the time from a DNS record or zone setting change until the Zone Builder finished writing to Quicksilver. It does not include Quicksilver's distribution across our network, which varies by location and is unaffected by this work. Production ran the old schedulers, and the mirror ran the unified scheduler on the same events over the same 24 hours. The two environments are identical apart from the code: they consume the same Kafka events, read from the same database, and write equivalent data to Quicksilver. That makes this a controlled, side-by-side comparison. The figures combine every build type and customer plan, so they are not a latency guarantee for an individual zone. A large share of this time is the rebuild interval described earlier, not build work. At each measurement point, p99 is the time within which 99% of events finished. Typical delays barely changed here, because most builds were already small. The difference is in the tail: the largest p99 spike fell from 14.6 minutes to 1.21 minutes, a 12-fold reduction. The chart uses a logarithmic scale. Targeted builds also load complete large zones far less often. Aggregate working-set memory, the memory actively used by the deployment, fell from an average of 49 GiB to 7 GiB, an 86% reduction. Peaks fell from 79 GiB to 12 GiB, an 85% reduction. Those were the immediate results of the new scheduler. They also let us revisit two safeguards. The first is the rebuild interval, which stops one busy zone from rebuilding constantly and taking capacity from everyone else. With builds now cheaper, and far fewer of them reading complete zones, we could safely shorten that interval on most plans. The second is how long the DNS Kafka Aggregator holds each event, to make sure database replicas have caught up before we read from them. Once our databases began rejecting reads from replicas that had fallen behind, that buffer could safely be smaller. Together, these halved the median build completion delay, from about 7.7 seconds to about 3.3 seconds. In the chart below, the first step down is the DNS Kafka Aggregator change. The red band marks the Zone Builder release with shorter rebuild intervals. That release rolled out gradually across our servers, so the delay falls in two further steps rather than all at once. The p90 and p99 lines in that chart are less precise than they look. The histogram had buckets at 1, 5, 10, and 30 seconds, and a percentile that falls between two edges is estimated as if delays were spread evenly across that range. Most delays sit near the bottom of their range, so those estimates come out high: p99 reads close to 30 seconds, and p90 above 7 seconds. The exact average, which does not depend on buckets, confirms the halving. We have since switched to a native histogram, which chooses fine-grained buckets automatically. It puts p90 at about 5.5 seconds and p99 at about 12 seconds. Why full builds still exist In 2022, we said we planned to eliminate full builds entirely. We now know that is neither realistic nor useful. A zone being published for the first time needs every record written. A change that can affect records anywhere in the zone needs every record checked. An event that does not say what changed still gets a full build, because the planner never turns uncertainty into less work. For a small zone, a full build is also cheap. As we learn what more events change, we will keep moving them to targeted builds. However, the biggest gain has already landed: the events that used to rebuild our largest zones no longer do, and the full builds that remain are mostly triggered by events, such as first publication, that affect new, small zones. items.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
items.author: Jack Clark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break – the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard: Realtime-Bench (official website). Read the paper: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv). *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.” Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people. “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”. “In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”. Space nukes: Russia is experimenting with nukes in space. “A nuclear detonation in space would create an electromagnetic pulse, which would immediately affect satellites within range and could impact civilian infrastructure,” the DIA writes. “A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits—LEO for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, GEO for critical communications, and MEO for navigation and timing satellites”. Why this matters – infrastructure for the next phase of the AI power struggle: As people spend more resources on building space-based data centers (and eventually, perhaps, lunar-based ones), space will become ever more strategically and commercially valuable and ever more contested. Research like this gives us a sense of the hardware which is already in space and will arrive in the future. Perhaps in some far-off future an AI might seek to take control of such space assets as well. Read more: DIA Releases Challenges to Security in Space (Defense Intelligence Agency, press release). Read the report: Challenges to Security in Space (DIA, PDF). *** Metis: A startup trying to fuse symbolic and neural reasoning: …Towards Vulcan-like machine minds… Metis, a startup that wants to build novel AI architectures oriented around developing machines with better reasoning, has published a research paper laying out its research approach. The high-level summary is simple – Metis wants to do for modern open-domain problems what DeepMind did for closed-domain problems like board games via its work on AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero. What they want to do: The key idea here is to add a reasoning core to modern AI architectures which is far more reliable than what we have today. “In modern AI architectures much of the other surrounding machinery that made AlphaGo a successful reasoning system remains either implicit or absent,” they write. “The first missing element is an explicit and persistent epistemic state… the second missing element is a criterion that allows the system to choose reasoning moves that make progress towards the goal.” This is more of a position paper than a technical paper, so they don’t have a ton of detail here. The main idea is to train a reasoning policy and value function based on real-world data collection, then use this to guide the system to perform reasoning that reduces long-term uncertainty, and have these sit on a basic core of data made up of claims or hypotheses about the world. “Any change to a claim’s evidential status must be licensed by evidence or verified through explicit calculation and approved by an independent judgment system,” they write. “Model-generated content cannot enter the accepted epistemic state merely by being plausible; it must pass warrant assessment, which lowers hallucinations. Sources of evidence can be attached directly to the propositions they support, providing a clear chain of provenance. The reasoning process becomes explicitly auditable.” Why this matters – building reliable substrates that are also deeply inhuman: Ideas like the architecture described here are fascinating both because of the promise they bring for increasing the reliability of AI systems, but also for how deeply inhuman they are: humans do not reason from some pristine base of facts, rather it’s all a big messy blob of memory and intuitions and some rules (some of which are learned from experience and some of which seem more platonic, like forms of logical reasoning). In this way, contemporary LLMs are more like humans than the system described here. “While the history of AI can be understood as a contest between symbolic and neural methods, it may be more constructive to view it as a story of two incomplete successes,” Metis writes. “Classical systems made aspects of the reasoning process explicit but depended on representations, operators, heuristics and knowledge supplied largely by hand. Contemporary LLMs learn extraordinary semantic operations and vast bodies of implicit knowledge but leave the organisation, evaluation and accumulation of reasoning implicit.” The AI system described here would ‘think’ in a way that is very different to how humans think and such a system might show us more about the differences between our own intelligence and that of machines. Read more: The Age of Reasoning (Metis, PDF). *** Google summons Genie 4 for better world modeling: …One of Google’s most interesting projects continues to live!… Google DeepMind has published details on Genie 4, a new iteration of its Genie world model. The company is rolling out access to Genie 4 currently as a research preview for some trusted testers and will eventually come to Google AI Ultra subscribers. The Genie series of models are fascinating, showing a world where you can take a photograph of anything and turn it into an interactable environment, or one where you can convert a 2D drawing into the stage for a videogame, and more. Key features: Google calls out four features that make Genie 4 different to previous ones. These include: Real-time modification: “You can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene.” Physics and human action simulation: “Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more,” and it also simulates people better. “The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time.” Sound modeling: “Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively,” Google writes. It also “introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly.” Simulating complex events: Google has embedded Gemini 3.8 Flash into Genie 4, so that the fast Flash model “serves as a guiding agent in the loop”, providing continual calibration. “Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning.” Why this matters – towards a multitude of worlds all dreamed up by machines: Though the technology is currently quite janky (e.g., robotic voices, a dreamlike sort of inconsistency in the visualized environments, etc), it points towards a world where we can generate infinite forms of entertainment (and potentially data?) via creating and prompting custom worlds. Read the announcement post: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind blog). Watch the video: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind, YouTube). Tech Tales: City Race [Description of a game played in the 2040s] One of the favorite games that children would play after The Uplift was called City Race; in it, they competed against one another to plan, build, and manage cities, expanding across the domain of a novel planet. The cities were trapped in time, starting with the technology of whatever era they were in, and the games took place over the course of about a century, allowing some further technology development to occur. Each game was played using a slice of the resources from the Dyson Swarm, allowing for a powerfully complex simulation (albeit with local-agent cognitive gating, such that nothing could develop enough sophistication to be deemed a Conscious Entity). Hundreds of thousands of simulated minds lived and died, sometimes thriving in cities run by careful and effective owners, and other times trapped in squalor, or growing old in places whose economies were hollowing out; casualties of the successes of others. It was deemed good for the children to learn what it meant to be gods, before they became adults. At the closure of every game, the children would need to spend a day living inside each of the cities in the gameworld they had played; those who had built marvelous cities experienced the wonders of their own creation, then walked through the broken towns whose success had been stymied by their own. Those who had struggled lived in their twilight towns, then got to tour the far off places that had doomed them. Things that inspired this story: Player of Games by Iain M Banks; Simcity; game playing; urban design; The Glass Bead Game by Hermann Hesse. Thanks for reading!

items.title: Independent Digital Media Is Not a Privilege Governments Can Revoke: The Fight to Save Egypt’s Mada Masr
items.author: Jillian C. York
items.content: On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists. The trial follows a conviction on October 27, when Attalah was found guilty of managing an unlicensed news website. The Mada Masr team had repeatedly applied for a license, but their attempts went unacknowledged. The proceedings took place in a single hearing, which Mada Masr states included serious violations of her right to a fair trial. She was sentenced to the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (approximately 55,000 USD), forcibly removed from the courtroom, and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered Mada Masr's closure and the confiscation of all equipment belonging to the organization. The current wave of repression has also targeted Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence initiative. Its entire six-person newsroom was violently arrested, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture before being charged with terrorism-related offenses and spreading false news. The team remains in pretrial detention. According to CPJ, at least 25 other journalists are currently incarcerated in Egypt. Governments seeking to control the flow of information increasingly rely on a combination of legal harassment, financial pressure, criminal prosecution, and restrictions on the infrastructure that makes independent publishing possible. Egypt's media licensing regime is a particularly troubling example. Requiring news organizations to obtain government authorization to operate creates an obvious mechanism for restricting who gets to publish and whose voices are allowed to reach the public. The charge of spreading false news is similarly dangerous. Governments around the world have increasingly invoked the language of misinformation to justify restrictions on speech, often without meaningful safeguards against political abuse, as we laid out in our recent submission to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Governments should never be the arbiters of which reporting is permissible, particularly when that reporting concerns their own conduct. Why Mada Masr matters Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has spent more than a decade doing the kind of journalism that authoritarian governments find most threatening: documenting abuses, amplifying marginalized voices, and reporting on issues that powerful institutions would prefer remain hidden. Its reporting has given torture survivors and the families of political prisoners a platform. It has opened space for debate about reproductive rights. It has brought frontline reporting from Sudan and Gaza, and stood alongside refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. Emerging as a digital-first publication, in a media environment where traditional outlets were increasingly constrained, being purely digital allowed Mada Masr’s founders to build an independent publication outside the structures of legacy media. At a time when only 43% of Egyptians had access to the internet, going fully digital meant taking a big risk, but it was one that has been rewarding: Despite being blocked by the Egyptian government since 2017, Mada Masr has continued to reach Egyptian and global audiences, and Attalah has received numerous accolades, including the Knight International Journalism Award, the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and a spot in TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential people (2020). Mada Masr has also consistently engaged with technology and advocated for a free and independent internet for the global majority. It has covered dozens of hot-button tech stories in recent years, from Egypt’s Cybercrime Bill and Israel’s use of AI weaponry in Gaza, to stories about the “privacy chaos” caused by biometrics to more personal essays about the importance of the internet and tech. In August, they launched an open call for proposals on original critical reporting on artificial intelligence. Mada Masr may be thoroughly Egyptian, but it doesn’t belong just to Egypt. Its team has made into a publication that represents the kind of independent, local, grounded journalism that international audiences need, particularly at a time when international reporting on state repression is lacking. They built on-the-ground networks to center local voices in Sudan (publishing in both English and Arabic on the conflict) and Gaza out of a sense of cross-border responsibility and solidarity. This is precisely why its potential closure should concern everyone who cares about a free press. The ability to publish independently, investigate powerful institutions, and to share information without government interference is fundamental to the exercise of free expression. From solidarity to action The international community has repeatedly expressed concern about restrictions on press and internet freedom in Egypt. More than 100 organizations have now joined statements of solidarity with Mada Masr, and with Matsada2sh. These expressions of support matter, particularly when journalists are increasingly isolated and under threat—but solidarity must also translate into sustained political and institutional pressure. The international governments and institutions that maintain relationships with Egypt—including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—should make clear that the prosecution of journalists and the forced closure of independent media outlets are unacceptable. The cases against Lina Attalah, Mada Masr, and Matsada2sh must be dropped. The journalists who remain in detention must be released. And Egypt's licensing regime, with its profound chilling effects on access to information and independent knowledge production, must be brought to an end. There is a particular urgency to defending independent media at a moment when governments are finding ever more ways to restrict the circulation of information. Whether through internet shutdowns, platform restrictions, surveillance, or the criminalization of reporting, the result is often the same: fewer opportunities for people to understand what is happening around them, to challenge official narratives, and to hold power accountable. We cannot allow the closure of one of Egypt's most important independent newsrooms and the prosecution of its editor-in-chief to become another routine episode in the global erosion of press freedom. Nor should we wait until the last independent journalists have been silenced before recognizing what has been lost. To learn more about Lina Attalah in her own reads, you can read our Speaking Freely interview from January 2026.

items.title: Why Peacock is making a huge bet on YouTube
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.content: Today, I’m talking with Matt Strauss, who is now chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. This is Matt’s second time joining me on the show, and there’s been a whole lot of organizational and structural change at NBCU since the last time he and I spoke just two years ago — pure Decoder bait. First, about a month after Matt was on the show, Comcast spun off most of the NBCU cable channels into something called Versant. That’s when Matt’s title changed from heading up just the direct-to-consumer offering — meaning Peacock, plus some other streaming services — to heading up the whole thing, across all distribution. And now, Comcast is spinning off the NBCU business entirely into a whole new standalone company. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. That’s a lot to have going on all at once! And meanwhile, it’s only just this year that Peacock became an actual profitable business at all — and it’s still pretty far away from being anything like the juggernaut that Netflix is. But what NBCU has, and what Peacock has, that the rest of the streaming industry is still trying to wrap its head around, is live sports. Sports are huge. They held up the cable industry for years, they held up broadcast, and now they’re the big thing that could make streaming a winner for NBC. One thing before we start: You’ll hear me ask Matt about the red company and the blue company. That’s just my way of getting Matt to talk about Netflix and Skydance, the company that now owns both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. I think he did a good job playing along. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Matt Strauss, chairman of the NBCU Media Group. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Matt Strauss, you are the chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. Welcome back to Decoder. Thank you so much, Nilay. It’s great to be back. I am very excited to talk to you. There’s a lot going on in the media. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood. I have to tell the audience that you and I are speaking minutes after Anthropic filed its S-1, and all of humanity is going to be turned into AI. Who knows what entertainment we’ll be watching in the future? There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the very beginning of this. You have a new job since last time you were on the show. Last time, you were the head of Direct-to-Consumer — you were basically the head of Peacock and the other apps inside the family. Now you’re the chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group. What’s the new job? What does that mean? NBCUniversal Media Group is comprised of certain services within NBC. It’s the broadcast network, it’s Bravo, it’s Peacock, it’s NBC Sports. We also have NBC News and Telemundo. One of the things that we recognized, especially when we spun off some of our cable assets last year into Versant, was that the assets we had truly worked better together. NBC has been like a megaphone. Given the reach of NBC, it’s been incredibly strategic in growing Peacock, which is a bit ironic because I think so many people believed that broadcasting was a bit of a relic of the past in this digital world, but it’s actually proven to be the opposite. As things have gotten more fragmented, having a broadcast network is actually a superpower because we’re continuing to see ratings growth. That has been really helpful as we’ve been building out Peacock. But actually, Peacock was also finding new audiences, like cord cutters or people who maybe didn’t grow up watching NBC or some of our cable networks. So, Peacock’s also been really strategic in reaching and driving people back to NBC and Bravo. So, I think that flywheel is where we recognized that we needed to start operating differently. I’ve been a huge advocate of what I like to call “centers of excellence” in how I like to structure the business, which is, content first and platform second. How do we get maximum reach, maximum engagement? That really required us thinking differently about how we were running the business. Essentially, instead of having a programming group within broadcast and a programming group within streaming, we just collapsed the business. Now you’ve got one programming team, one marketing team, one product and technology team, one decision sciences and research team, and one advertising team. They’re all incentivized around continuing to grow the portfolio, get that maximum reach, maximum engagement, and drive top-line revenue. I think that structure, which we put in place about 18 months ago, is contributing to a lot of the success that we’re seeing now. Even if you look at 2026, NBC is the number one network in total viewers. We had an unbelievable early part of the year with “Legendary February,” which you might remember. That’s when we had the Super Bowl, the Milan Cortina Olympics, and the NBA All-Star Game. In 17 days, we reached over 225 million viewers. This summer, we had Love Island, which was the number one show of the summer for streaming. You had the World Cup, which was the number one Spanish-language sporting event in US history on Telemundo and Peacock. We had a show called The Five-Star Weekend, which was our number one scripted drama. Now, we’ve led ourselves into the fall, where we have Sunday Night Football, which has been the number one show for 15 consecutive years. We had a great kickoff with over 25 million viewers. We just had the NBA tip-off last week with the Knicks and the Sixers, which is the number one rated tip-off in NBA history. So, it does feel like we’re firing on all cylinders in how we’re trying to operate with this, again, content-first-platform-second mantra. But just to go one level deeper, a big part of this strategy is figuring out how do we move audiences across platforms. For example, when I mentioned that Love Island was the number one streaming show of the summer, 40 percent of those Love Island viewers also tuned in to watch the World Cup. So, migrating viewers back and forth across the portfolio is a critical part of how we see ourselves continuing to grow. But to effectuate that, you need to structure yourself in a way where people are incentivized along that vision. We’re still evolving as an organization, but I’m really proud of some of the milestones and accomplishments that we’ve made as a team. I love my job. I feel like I’ve got the best job in the industry at the moment. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood, and you seem like one of the happiest people in the industry right at the second. That is very notable. You’re a Decoder pro, you brought up structure. I’m dying to ask you about the Decision Sciences Group. That’s the other question I ask everybody. But let me just back out for one second. You’re describing quite a lot of freedom in rethinking how something like NBCUniversal would work. You mentioned the Versant spin, so CNBC, MS Now, and a bunch of channels went that way. I’m on its networks all the time. I would describe the folks at Versant as feeling more free. They’re disconnected from the battleship that was Comcast and NBCUniversal. They can go try whatever they want to try. They’re energized by it in some ways. Then, Comcast looked at NBCUniversal and said, “We’re going to spin off that off as well. We’re going to be the cable business and NBCUniversal will be the entertainment business, and now you’re in charge of that.” You’re like a 20-year Comcast veteran. I think you got your start doing cable boxes. Yep. I started in 2004 at Comcast. Just tell me about that process. We spun off CNBC and MS Now into Versant. Now we’re looking at this company. We ought to spin off NBCUniversal as well. Just tell me about how that came about. What was that moment like? Did you all sit in a boardroom? Did it come down from on high? How did that happen? Well, that decision really was made by Brian Roberts and Mike Cavanagh. Candidly, I was not in the room when that decision was made, but I think if you were to ask people at NBCUniversal, it makes strategic sense. Do you feel that same sense of freedom? You know what? I think that there’s an energy. When people show up here, they feel very passionate about what they do. They believe in our strategy, they believe in our portfolio. Look at NBCUniversal more broadly.
