Somebody watched that show, and it was on six days a week. When the show is over, what we do and what every streaming service does is we say, “Oh, you like this show? You should watch another show. You should watch The Real Housewives.” But that’s not what a lot of these viewers wanted. What they wanted at the end of the show was to talk about what just happened. So, they leave the streaming platform and go to social media, they’ll look for a podcast, or they’ll even play a game if they could. By the way, the number one app over the summer was the Love Island app. It was not ChatGPT. It was not Claude. It was the Love Island app for several weeks over the summer. That speaks to what I’m describing around these fandoms. We are creating this demand, but I would argue we’re not doing a good enough job super-serving them. Then, we are fueling this what I would call “dark matter engagement” on these other platforms. This is what’s leading us to say, “What if we put the clips on Peacock and we offer it in a vertical video format? What if we create a podcast for Love Island? What if we create gaming?” But it’s not any game. These games are derivatives of the fandoms and content that we have on our platform. Can we better super-serve those fans and then grow our share of time? I think that’s the opportunity. That’s the ambition. It doesn’t mean that we’re not going to work with YouTube, TikTok, Reels, or other platforms. I would argue that the best place for our content, franchises, IP should be on our platforms. But to do that, you have to expand the aperture of what you deliver as a platform, which is why I think streaming is too limiting. You should really think of it more as an entertainment platform designed to maximize share of time and retention. I think the partnership we announced with YouTube this summer is going to be an example of how we see ourselves continuing to drive more of that audience and engagement across our platform but also working very closely with YouTube. That YouTube deal looks like the rebundling you’re talking about, right? Peacock will be available to YouTube Premium subscribers. I have YouTube TV. I imagine that will somehow connect the dots. YouTube is fascinating because it has the user-generated content platform and TV. Those things are starting to compete with each other, right? I look at the viewership charts, and classic, user-generated YouTube is skyrocketing, just eating up everyone’s time all day long. Everyone has to be there. I’m assuming the economics of YouTube TV look like cable for you. They have to be far more lucrative. When you go into a room with [YouTube CEO] Neil Mohan and say, “Well, there’s the platform that’s very lucrative and there’s a platform I have to be on,” how do you reconcile the economics of the two? From my point of view, it’s not one or the other. It’s both. It comes back to what I said about how they’re not exactly the same audiences. There’s some overlap, but somebody who is subscribing to YouTube TV is not necessarily the same person who is subscribing to YouTube Premium or consuming content on main YouTube. I agree with you that when you look at this through the share of time lens, YouTube has done an unbelievable job creating a platform and business model that allows it to continue to grow. I don’t see anything that would indicate that’s going to slow down. When you look at it from my point of view, so much of our content and IP lives on YouTube in some form, whether it’s SNL or Love Island, whether it’s clips from The Traitors or any of our NBC shows. But those viewers don’t necessarily subscribe to Peacock. They don’t necessarily watch NBC or Bravo. So, I think that was the opportunity. That was the unlock. How actually can we transform ourselves to reimagine what it could look like to partner with YouTube? One of the things that I was talking about earlier with this great rebundling — which we talked about and somewhat predicted seven years ago — was that the one thing that held the bundle together in cable television for many years was sports. What you don’t want to do is a bundle deal without getting the right underlying wholesale economics. What will happen is that you could take a very high ARPU, direct-to-consumer subscriber and end up cannibalizing them for a low, wholesale bundled subscriber. What you’re really looking for is incrementality. Is this going to drive incremental subscribers, and can I get the right wholesale economics where this is also incremental on the revenue side? What’s interesting about YouTube is that I think it’s a win-win. It’s a win-win because there’s multiple components to this deal. One aspect is that there’s going to be a bundle launched next year with the ad-supported tier of Peacock and a tier of YouTube Premium. Now, you’re going to get access to all of the benefits of YouTube Premium with the ad-supported version of Peacock. We believe that these are mostly incremental subscribers, or people who do not necessarily have Peacock today. So, it’s going to grow Peacock while adding more value to YouTube Premium. My prediction is that if you and I have a conversation a year from now, Peacock will be one of the top distributed streaming services in the United States. Do you care that you don’t own your last-mile customer that way? This was a big reason everyone went to streaming. They were selling their content to Netflix, and they realized Netflix owned the customer. Now we’ve all got to stand up our own streaming services because we want to own the customer and the cable bundle is falling apart. Do you care now that as you rebundle, YouTube will own the customer in some important way? I think that when you say “own the customer,” really what you’re talking about is, “How do I get the ability to personalize the experience so that I could super-serve an individual both with content and with advertising? What’s ultimately going to create the monetization engine that we need?” I was describing the value of Peacock and the fact that 80 percent of our subs are on the ad platform and that we typically charge premium CPMs (cost per mille) because we have this ability to super-serve our fandoms and franchises, and we have the data to do it. I think that the relationship with YouTube that we announced this summer is going to allow us to have a much deeper integration with YouTube on the data side as well as the integration with FreeWheel. So, we’re at a point where we’re almost indifferent again about where somebody consumes the content— FreeWheel is your programmatic advertising business. Yes. That was a critical part to this unlock with YouTube because we can create a bundle that is going to drive incremental subscribers and value. To your point, YouTube TV is the fastest-growing pay TV distributor. I think the pay TV ecosystem has been declining at a 6-7 percent CAGR. Over the past five years, YouTube TV has grown at a 26-27 percent CAGR. It has over 10 million subscribers and are likely going to be the number one pay TV distributor in the next couple of years. We extended our linear portfolio agreement with YouTube TV, which is going to provide us stability and growth on that part of our portfolio as well. What we were just describing around having a much deeper integration with the data, analytics, and targeting is going to allow us to monetize our inventory. It’s all of these pieces. We think this is an example of how we’re trying to think differently, or how we’re trying to be innovative and identify strategic partners. I don’t know if the red company or the blue company would be in a position to do the kind of deal that I’m describing, but it’s precisely because we are independent and looking to be more flexible. I think that actually becomes a calling card for how we could work with other companies in a way that is really transformative. Let me ask you, I think the red company hypothetically got turned upside down because it relied on data too much for the programming and now it’s going to change a bunch of programming executives, so we’ll see where it goes. The hypothetical blue company led by the hypothetical son of a billionaire is out in the market. It made a big content acquisition. He’s saying, “Oh, we’re going to invest in technology and we’ll compete with Northern California. We’ll compete with any of the platforms based on our technology bet.” To me, that seems like an old story where I know the ending. Trying to run at TikTok’s technology without the content is just going to get you backwards. If you were running the blue company, how would you think about technology in that way? Well, I’m going to answer the question based on how I’m running our company. The blue company’s new. Anything could happen with the blue company. I think my answer, though, would not change depending on where I sat within this industry. I believe that we need to be an open ecosystem, that you’ve got to go where the viewers are. That’s what led us to make a lot of strategic decisions, whether it’s the deal that I just described with YouTube, or the channel deals for the ad-free tier of Peacock with Amazon and Roku. We’ve done bundling deals. We’ve done a bundle deal with Apple. We’ve done a bundle deal with Walmart. You’re trying to give consumers choices. Everything I’ve done in my career has always been around the north star of giving consumers choice: what they want, when they want, where they want. That, to me, has been the mantra for how we’re trying to build our company. All of that being said, I am still also a huge believer in the product, the technology, and the experience. You may be able to watch the Olympics on another platform through NBC or Peacock, but I truly believe the best experience was on Peacock. Are you allowed to say that on other people’s networks? Can you go on to Amazon channels and say, “This is great, but if you want the first class, get out of this app and open Peacock?” Do they let you say that? Well, I wouldn’t say it that way, though. First of all, I think when somebody subscribes to Peacock, they should be able to access our service regardless of the platform. In that respect, we do cross-authentication — meaning you can subscribe and watch on Peacock, or you could subscribe and access our service through channels. I’m not here to tell the consumer what the best experience is. I think that we lead by example. The consumers vote based on where they ultimately decide to engage. If you want to get access to some of these cool features that I’m describing, if you want to play a game that we created, or if you want to listen to a podcast, or… I’ll give you another example. We’re testing our membership program because we shouldn’t think of viewers as subscribers, we should think of them as members. What are the other values that you can get as part of being a member? Well, maybe some of those values could be based on your tenure or your level of engagement. Maybe you get discounts to NBC merchandise. Maybe you get special access when you go to Universal theme parks. Maybe you get discounts from some of our advertising partners, like Domino’s. How do we start to add more value? But maybe that membership is only available when you’re on our platform. I think of it more as needing to give consumers the choice. At the same time, we are investing in product and technology and on experiences that are really meant to be delivered upon the platform that we have created. We’ve got an unbelievable team, in my opinion, that has created a best-in-class, scalable platform that not only powers Peacock, but also powers Sky’s Now TV. It’s the same platform that we’ve also distributed to dozens of countries around the world. We’ve got a world-class team that is really trying to transform, surprise, and delight viewers in a way that I’m not sure other platforms are going to be able to do around our content and franchises, especially when it comes to especially these major tentpole events. I want to end by asking maybe the most important question of all. We’re talking a lot about internet-distributed businesses and consumers signing up for services and being able to churn and quit. There are a lot of free market dynamics there, which I think are very powerful and very important. That means you get to program whatever you want to program. You have chosen live in sports and, importantly, you mentioned news at the top of this conversation. NBC News is part of this portfolio. NBC News is also distributed over broadcast. It’s distributed over the air. The Trump administration and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, in particular, has expressed a lot of desire to pressure broadcast networks because you use the public spectrum, particularly news networks. He’s withheld the broadcast licenses for ABC stations, for example. He has threatened the other broadcast networks. There’s a lot of pressure on NBC News. How are you handling that? Are you pushing back? Because that is the one place where you’re not allowed to just do whatever you want, right? The government gets to tell you what to say in an increasingly uncomfortable way. Yeah. Look, I think I give a lot of credit to [NBCUniversal News Group Chairman] Cesar Conde and the NBC News organization who are big believers in freedom of speech and freedom of the press. I think they’re doing a fantastic job. When it comes to distribution of our content, especially our news programming, I think that’s an example where it’s available everywhere. I mean, we truly make it available not only on Peacock, NBC, and over the air, but through Fast TV, NBC News Now— Have you made this argument to the administration? Because I’ve met a lot of FCC chairmen over the years, and until Carr showed up, the argument they would make is that we have to get away from overthinking broadcast because the audience is everywhere, and they don’t actually make a distinction between broadcast television and cable. That was a Republican talking point for years and years. This is nonsense. The other version is that everyone’s on TikTok and the industry has to contend with that in some way. We should get more people internet access because that will actually even the playing field. Now we’ve come to, “You have to use the spectrum in the public interest.” It is different and the government should impose some speech pressure — which again, I think is inappropriate — but that is a new argument. I’m wondering if you have said to the administration, “Look, the consumer doesn’t make this distinction and we as a company aren’t making this distinction.” Well, I’ve not had those direct conversations myself. Obviously, we have a government affairs team that works very closely with regulators in DC. There’s probably no better time to be alive than right now when it comes to being able to access content through multiple modalities, whether it’s over-the-air broadcast, social media platforms, or free. If you were to look at Peacock, not only do we distribute NBC News, we distribute all of our own stations as well. I could be watching the Los Angeles local news in New York or I could be watching the Philadelphia local news. There’s no shortage of ways that we are supporting the public good in giving them multiple ways and choices in how they want to consume and access their news programming, and I don’t think that’s going to change. I think we’re going to continue to advocate for freedom of speech and freedom of the press. I think our news organization has been doing an unbelievable job in the product and the service that they’re doing for the public. Yeah. Matt, you can tell that’s an important topic for me for a lot of reasons. What’s next for NBCUniversal Media Group? What’s next for Peacock? What should people be looking for? I think what’s next for NBCUniversal Media Group is, as we talked about, we will likely be a separate company as part of the new NBC this time next year. You’ve got to come back. There’s a bunch of questions where I knew I wasn’t going to get answers because the deal isn’t closed yet. When that closes, you’ve got to come back because I have a million questions. I will definitely come back. I’m really looking forward to it. I think the other piece, as you know, is that we had our Q3 earnings last week. We talked a lot about Peacock and how we had a very different strategy with Peacock from the others when we launched our service six years ago. I’m really proud to share that Peacock was profitable in Q3 for the second consecutive quarter. We had $261 million of EBITDA. That’s $470 million better year-over-year. I think the team has done an unbelievable job, and I feel really good about our momentum and continuing to grow. It’s good proof that there’s not one way to go to market. There’s not one strategy or approach. You’ve got to play your hand and to your strengths, and you’re going to see us continue to do that at NBCUniversal. Yeah. We didn’t even talk about what AI might do to the cost structure of video. When you come back, we’re going to get into it. Matt, thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thank you so much. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Duet + How Figma’s PMs actually use AI every day
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.content: Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: which one crushes the competition? Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more Firecrawl—Give your AI agents web data and beyond In this solo episode, Claire puts Grok Bot, Dot, Meta’s Muse, and Claude Duet through nine real-world tasks to find out which personal agents are actually worth using. She tests them on everything from Slack replies, inbox triage, and coding to video editing, Figma thumbnails, family projects, and shopping. The results point to a clear split. Biggest takeaways: Grok Bot is the strongest all-around personal agent in this benchmark, especially for work. It scored 93% overall and won the Figma, inbox triage, and shopping tasks. For someone choosing one agent for professional workflows, Claire recommends starting here. Muse is the best agent for personal life. It created the strongest short-form video and family newspaper with almost no prompting and answered a physics question too quickly to time. That speed has led Claire to move more quick Q&A conversations from ChatGPT to Muse. Speed is central to the product experience. Muse finished first on four of the nine tasks, while Claude Duet was consistently the slowest. When an agent disappears for several minutes, users lose context and stop wanting to use it. Claude Duet asks for permission too often. It requested approval four times during the benchmark, compared with once for every other agent. That caution may be well-intentioned, but it makes Duet feel like something the user must supervise rather than trust. An agent is only as capable as the tools it can access. A Codex audit found that Claire’s agents did not have equivalent connectors and skills. Muse lacked Slack and GitHub, which prevented it from completing several work tasks, highlighting the importance of equal setups for a fair comparison. Grok Bot is the agent Claire trusts most with Figma. Dot and Claude Duet mostly filled existing templates, while Grok Bot proposed fresh headlines and layouts that looked like real YouTube thumbnails. It has consistently outperformed the others across Claire’s Figma tests. Claude Duet and Dot still showed the strongest coding judgment. Dot came closest to the intended Sentry fix, while Duet found a second bug and avoided duplicating work Dot had already completed. Claire would still choose Claude or Codex for serious coding, just not through Duet’s personal-agent interface. Dot showed the strongest personal context in one important moment. It was the only agent that asked whether Claire’s Lovable talk was paid and remote, which felt like genuine chief-of-staff judgment. Its poor performance on creative tasks, however, kept it well behind Grok Bot and Muse overall. The useful takeaway is that different agents belong in different parts of life. Claire’s current split is Grok Bot for work and Muse for personal tasks. Choosing agents by job is more effective than expecting one product to handle everything well. Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode: Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: Nine Tasks, Four Agents, No Universal Winner: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/grok-vs-dot-vs-muse-vs-claude-duet-nine-tasks-four-agents-no-universal-winner ↳ Generate Novel YouTube Thumbnail Ideas with Grok and Figma: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/generate-novel-youtube-thumbnail-ideas-with-grok-and-figma ↳ How to Create a Branded Product Launch Video with Claude Duet: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/how-to-create-a-branded-product-launch-video-with-claude-duet ↳ Create a Personalized Family Newspaper with Meta’s Muse: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/create-a-personalized-family-newspaper-with-meta-s-muse How Figma’s PMs actually use AI every day | Ezra Mechaber (PM, Figma) Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: Optimizely—Your AI agent orchestration platform for marketing and digital teams Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence Ezra Mechaber is a growth product manager at Figma and one of the creators of PM OS, a shared repository of 31 AI skills used across the company’s product organization. In this episode, he demonstrates how Figma’s PMs use it to manage Slack, gather organizational context, create artifacts, and run more thorough bug bashes with Codex. He also walks through AutoXP, an AI growth PM that runs experiments with a single human checkpoint, and a real-time Jev assistant that improves writing as he types. Biggest takeaways: The best place to start with AI is the work PMs routinely skip. Ezra designed PM OS around tasks that fall through the cracks, such as involving support before a launch or documenting meetings. His goal is to establish a minimum acceptable standard for every PM workflow. Context-gathering skills are the foundation of useful AI at work. At a company with roughly 2,000 employees, even identifying the right collaborators can be difficult. One PM OS skill maps a team and automatically adds the relevant designer, engineering manager, and team leaders as reviewers. A simple “what’s up” skill can make Slack manageable. Ezra runs it about six times a day to gather relevant threads, projects, open decisions, and people awaiting a response. He archives roughly 10 channels daily because the skill preserves what actually matters. A basic Git repository can support an entire PM organization. PM OS consists of an AGENTS.md file, reusable skills, and a few command hooks. An automatic version check keeps 60 to 70 PMs aligned, while private subrepositories give each person room to customize. Successful AI adoption starts with familiar tools, then evolves with users. PM OS began as a terminal interface in Claude Code before gaining a local web interface that was easier to read. Ezra now works primarily in Codex, partly because browser use has become reliable enough for his workflow. Agents can be more diligent bug bashers than humans. Ezra gives his agent a test account and a FigJam board full of scenarios, then has it document its findings. It has caught edge cases ranging from a text box filled with 1,000 emojis to grammar that changed based on a team’s name. In growth, wasted traffic is the biggest sin. AutoXP uses three agents to identify funnel drop-off, propose new copy, and prepare the implementation. A human reviews the experiment once before launch, after which the system analyzes results and begins the next iteration automatically. Fast, inexpensive models can provide feedback that feels continuous. Ezra’s Jev prototype reviews writing whenever the user pauses, flags placeholders and unsupported claims, and finds relevant interview quotes from a research library. The speed makes it feel less like running an AI task and more like working beside an attentive editor. When an AI conversation goes bad, starting over often beats arguing with it. Ezra treats poor output as a sign of unclear instructions or contaminated context. He opens a fresh conversation, restates the goal, and approaches the model with high expectations: “Buddy, I know you can cook.” Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode: Inside Figma’s PM OS: 31 AI Skills, Better Bug Bashes, and an Automated Growth Loop: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/inside-figma-s-pm-os-31-ai-skills-better-bug-bashes-and-an-automated-growth-loop ↳ Automate Software Bug Bashing with a Browser Agent: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/automate-software-bug-bashing-with-a-browser-agent ↳ Build an Automated Growth Experiment Loop with Multiple AI Agents: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-an-automated-growth-experiment-loop-with-multiple-ai-agents ↳ Build a Personal PM Operating System with a Shared Knowledge Repo: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-a-personal-pm-operating-system-with-a-shared-knowledge-repo If you’re enjoying these episodes, reply and let me know what you’d love to learn more about: AI workflows, hiring, growth, product strategy—anything. Catch you next week, Lenny P.S. Want every new episode delivered the moment it drops? Hit “Follow” on your favorite podcast app.

items.title: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)
items.author: Daniel Abib
items.content: The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x. Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed. How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog. Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.
